content: The recommended dosage of powdered licorice root (Glycyrrhiza glabra) for specific indications is 5 to 10 grams taken orally, one to three times daily (qD-TID). The duration of use should not exceed 4 to 6 weeks. Licorice is used for a variety of conditions, including adrenocortical insufficiency, arthritis, bronchitis, dry cough, peptic ulcers, gastritis, bacterial and viral infections, prostate cancer, sore throat, systemic lupus erythematosus, and upper respiratory inflammation. Licorice has been shown to increase the effects of digoxin through pharmacodynamic synergism. However, the clinical significance of this interaction is considered minor or unknown. Adverse effects associated with licorice include amenorrhea, congestive heart failure (CHF), decreased libido, edema, erectile dysfunction, headache, hypertension, hypertensive encephalopathy, hypokalemia, hypokalemic myopathy, lethargy, lower extremity weakness, mineralocorticoid effects, myoglobinuria, pulmonary edema, quadriplegia, rhabdomyolysis, sodium and fluid retention, and other related conditions. Licorice is contraindicated in individuals with breast cancer, cholestatic liver disorders, cirrhosis, CHF, diabetes mellitus, endometriosis, hormone-sensitive conditions, hypertonia, hypersensitivity to licorice, hypertension, hypokalemia, ovarian cancer, severe renal insufficiency, uterine cancer, and uterine fibroids. It should also be avoided in patients taking CYP3A4 substrates or potassium-depleting agents, as well as those with impaired liver function. The FDA has issued a consumer alert regarding licorice consumption: consuming more than 2 ounces per day for at least 2 weeks may lead to hypokalemia and arrhythmias, particularly in adults aged 40 or older. Licorice is classified as unsafe during pregnancy and should be avoided during lactation. While some substances are generally considered safe during pregnancy (Category A), licorice does not fall into this category. Controlled studies in pregnant women have not demonstrated safety, and its use is not recommended. Licorice exhibits anti-inflammatory and expectorant properties. It inhibits the metabolism of prostaglandins PGE2 and PGF2-alpha. However, deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) is less effective for upper respiratory conditions. No specific data are available regarding the metabolism or excretion of licorice.
